 View Comments Milwaukee Brewers right fielder Sal Frelick warns up prior to Game 1 of baseball's National League Championship Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Los Angeles Dodgers, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Abbie Parr) Abbie Parr/AP Photo/Abbie Parr MILWAUKEE — Sal Frelick was a first-round draft pick of the Milwaukee Brewers in 2021 out of Boston College and made his major league debut two years later. 
 He has since played on four division winners and appeared in 19 postseason games. It has been only consistent success since the 26-year-old outfielder put on a Brewers uniform. 
 So Frelick does not share the national perception of this World Series between the Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays as a matchup of overachieving teams with modest payrolls. 
 “We’re a good team that has been building in this direction,” Frelick said Thursday on the eve of Game 1 at American Family Field. “There is nothing surprising about this. Ever since I got drafted, ever since I debuted, we’ve been trying to get here. Now we want to go win it.” 
 Still, it’s hard to ignore the financial side of the Series with Major League Baseball’s collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. The league is widely expected to lock the players out , and the dispute could carry on for months.

 That makes this an ill-timed matchup for commissioner Rob Manfred. Milwaukee’s $154.7 million luxury tax payroll ranked 19th in the league and the Rays, at $113.2 million, were 27th. The Brewers swept the $433 million Dodgers in the NLCS and the Rays bounced the $341.8 million Yankees in three games in the AL Division Series. 
 “Just two good teams regardless of payroll,” Frelick said. 
 This will be a memorable World Series in some way. The Brewers and Rays are two of the five teams that have never won a championship. The Mariners, Padres, and Rockies are the others. 
 This will be the first Series in which two teams are seeking their first title since the Phillies beat the Royals in 1980. The 2023 Rangers and 2019 Nationals were the most recent first-time champions. 
 Sal Frelick grew up a Red Sox fan in Lexington. But he'll play in his first World Series with the Brewers. "This is what you dream of as a kid," he said. Kayla Wolf/Associated Press Frelick grew up a Red Sox fan in Lexington and experienced World Series championships from that angle. Now he has the opportunity to make history of his own. 
 “This is what you dream of as a kid,” Frelick said. “It’s just been fun. Playing with this group of guys, too, has been great.” 
 The Brewers haven’t played since finishing their stunning sweep of the Dodgers on Oct. 15. Their seven-day layoff is the longest for any World Series team since the 2007 Rockies, who were off for eight days before facing the Red Sox. 
 The Sox pounded the Rockies, 13-1 , in Game 1 and went on to a four-game sweep . Colorado led for only three innings in that Series. The Brewers guarded against that by taking only a few days off. 
 “We played baseball; that’s how we prepared,” manager Pat Murphy said. “We went out there and played baseball every day, live at-bats. You can’t recreate real; you know what I mean? It’s a long layoff, and if we want to use it as an excuse, then let people use it as an excuse, but I refuse to do that.” 
 The extra time helped Frelick. He was on the injured list from July 18-Aug. 25 with a strained right shoulder. The injury, which started bothering him in June, was diagnosed as a torn labrum. Frelick doesn’t believe he will need surgery after the season. 
 But his shoulder was clearly a problem. Frelick hit .288 with a .756 OPS last season and was fourth among Brewers position players with 2.9 bWAR. That dropped to .230 with a .614 OPS this season. 
 “Obviously it was hurt,” Frelick said. “I had to deal with it, and it’s good to go now. During the season it affected me, but we took care of it, and I’m fine now, as good as I can be.” 
 If Murphy sticks with the lineup construction he has used in the postseason, the lefthanded-hitting Frelick will be in the lineup against Rays righthander Nick Martinez on Friday night. 
 Frelick played baseball, football, and hockey at Lexington High. He was a three-time Globe All-Scholastic in baseball and twice in football as a quarterback. Frelick accepted a scholarship to BC intending to play football and baseball before deciding to focus on the latter. 
 As Frelick was preparing for Game 1, people gathered outside Hayden Ice Rink in Lexington on Thursday to rally in support of their hometown hero. Nearby Worthen Road has been renamed Sal Frelick Way for the duration of the Series. 
 If Frelick returns home with a championship, maybe that should become permanent.
